1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Basic information: The patient was a 46-year-old woman who was admitted to our hospital on Day 0, with the chief complaints of "chest tightness, shortness of breath, and lower extremity edema." In approximately 21 months before Day 0, without an obvious precipitating factor, this female patient developed edema of both lower extremities and the face, as well as chest tightness and shortness of breath. She could not tolerate ordinary activities. Symptoms worsened in the supine position and improved after sitting up. There was no urinary urgency, frequency, or dysuria; no nausea or vomiting; and no chest pain, cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, etc. She had previously been seen in the cardiology and respiratory departments of Yan'an Hospital and was diagnosed with "congenital heart disease"; she improved after treatment and was discharged. She was hospitalized twice in 2004. When her condition was stable, she was able to manage activities of daily living, but she developed shortness of breath after walking long distances or climbing one flight of stairs. More than 10 days before admission, her symptoms worsened, and she was admitted to the cardiology department of our hospital. During hospitalization in cardiology, after treatment with cardiotonic therapy, diuresis, vasodilators, and oxygen therapy, the patient developed clouding of consciousness. Emergent arterial blood gas analysis showed: pH 7.15↓, PO₂ 88mmHg↓, PCO₂ 120mmHg↑. After emergency endotracheal intubation, PCO₂ was 48mmHg; later, the patient self-extubated. She was then transferred to the respiratory department of our hospital and admitted with "pulmonary hypertension, cause to be determined; type II respiratory failure." Physical examination on admission: T: 36.8℃, R: 25 breaths/min, P: 98 beats/min, BP: B110/80mmHg, poor general condition. Moderate cyanosis of the lips while on oxygen. Jugular venous distention throughout the course in the supine position. Coarse breath sounds in both lungs, with a small amount of moist rales audible at both lower lungs. Cardiac dullness enlarged bilaterally, heart rate 96 beats/min, irregular rhythm, P2 > A2. Hepatomegaly, palpable 4 cm below the xiphoid process and 3 cm below the right costal margin. No edema of both lower extremities. Relevant examinations were completed: Day 0 arterial blood gas: PH 7.27↓, PO₂ 41mmHg ↓, PCO₂ 84mmHg↑, BE 8.9, FI 21%. CBC: WBC 10.44x10^9/L, Hb146g/L, platelets 138x10^9/L. Chemistry: renal function and electrolytes normal; lactate 4.2mmol/L (0.7-2.1 mmol/L). ECG: sinus rhythm, right atrial overload, T-wave changes. Chest X-ray: cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension; infiltrative lesion in the right lower lung field. Cardiac echocardiography on 2025 Day -6: enlargement of the right atrium and right ventricle; widening of the main pulmonary artery and right pulmonary artery; mild regurgitation of the tricuspid valve and pulmonary valve; normal left ventricular systolic function. Moderate to severe pulmonary arterial pressure 66mmHg. The patient left the respiratory department against medical advice after 2 days of hospitalization and died 2 years after discharge. Twenty years later, her younger brother came to our hospital. The following is her brother's condition: Liu XX, male, 59 years old, Han ethnicity, retired teacher. Chief complaint: exercise intolerance for more than 40 years, dyspnea accompanied by snoring during sleep for more than 3 years. History of present illness: ① More than 40 years ago, the patient developed dyspnea during long-distance running, weakness of the extremities, decreased running distance, and difficulty climbing mountains and going uphill; ② he developed left ptosis, deviation of the corner of the mouth to the left, tongue deviation to the left on protrusion, and decreased hearing in the left ear; facial paralysis was considered, and he recovered 6 months later; ③ more than 3 years ago, he developed dyspnea after mild activity accompanied by snoring during sleep, with snoring not loud, nocturnal awakenings 3-4 times/night, light sleep, morning dizziness, non-restorative sleep, and daytime sleepiness. He sought care at Fuwai Cardiovascular Hospital, where relevant examinations were completed, and was diagnosed with "severe obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, metabolic cardiomyopathy, mitochondrial disease?" Treatment with a ventilator was recommended, but the patient refused. He now presents to our department because of worsening dyspnea and palpitations. Past medical history: 4 years ago, the patient developed stomach pain and acid regurgitation, and gastroesophageal reflux was considered. 2 years ago, because of tachycardia, he underwent cardiac radiofrequency ablation. No history of tobacco or alcohol use. No surgical history. Developmental history: no special circumstances during pregnancy, full-term birth, normal delivery process, normal language and behavioral development in infancy and early childhood. Family history: his mother died at age 40, 3 days after surgery for rectal cancer; no similar symptoms were identified before her death. His father died at age 68 of cor pulmonale. One elder sister was small and thin and had a similar history to the patient, with many years of exercise intolerance and dyspnea, multiple episodes of hypercapnic coma, and died of respiratory failure of unknown cause at age 48. He denied similar medical history in other family members and denied consanguinity. General condition fair, clear consciousness, vital signs stable, height: 164cm, weight: 48kg, BMI: 17.84Kg/㎡, small and thin build, decreased hearing in the left ear, mild cyanosis of the lips, slightly narrow pharyngeal cavity, flat chest, slightly diminished breath sounds, no dry or moist rales, no pleural friction rub. No abnormalities found on cardiac or abdominal examination. No edema of both lower extremities. No obvious cranial nerve abnormalities, hip flexion muscle strength of both lower extremities grade 4+, muscle strength of the remaining limbs grade 5, decreased deep tendon reflexes in all extremities, no pathologic signs elicited, no abnormalities in sensation or coordination, meningeal irritation signs negative. Psychiatric examination: consciousness clear, orientation intact, good contact, answers relevant to questions, no obvious psychotic symptoms elicited, affect appropriate, insight present, social functioning normal. Examinations before admission: PSG: 1. severe obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome; 2. severe nocturnal hypoxemia. AHI 46.5 events/hour; predominantly obstructive hypopnea events; lowest oxygen saturation 30%. Muscle biopsy electron microscopy: muscle biopsy pathology examination: In 2021, at an outside hospital cardiovascular medicine department: biochemical tests: LAC 8.08.0mmol/L↑, creatine kinase 124 U/L↑, creatinine 41umol/L↓. Muscle biopsy: RRF/ragged blue fibers seen; electron microscopy showed lattice-like mitochondria and other abnormal mitochondria. Preliminary diagnoses: 1. obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome; 2. respiratory failure; 3. metabolic cardiomyopathy; 4. pulmonary hypertension; 5. reflux esophagitis; 6. hyperuricemia; 7. decreased hearing in the left ear; 8. mitochondrial disease?

differential_diagnoses.name: Alveolar hypoventilation syndrome (caused by neuromuscular disease/respiratory muscle involvement) with type II respiratory failure
supporting_evidence: The phase 1 text shows that the patient had significant hypercapnia and acidosis: pH 7.15, PCO2 120 mmHg; repeat arterial blood gas still showed pH 7.27, PO2 41 mmHg, PCO2 84 mmHg, consistent with severe type II respiratory failure.

The patient’s symptoms are mainly chest tightness, dyspnea, and decreased exercise tolerance, which worsen in the supine position and improve after sitting up, suggesting ventilatory limitation or abnormal respiratory mechanics.

Pulmonary examination revealed only a small number of moist rales at both lower lungs; pulmonary symptoms were not prominent, but hypercapnia was very severe, suggesting that the degree of gas exchange impairment was not entirely consistent with the pulmonary auscultatory findings.

In the first-stage text, his younger brother had long-term exercise intolerance, dyspnea, snoring during sleep, respiratory failure, and “mitochondrial disease?”; another older sister also had a similar medical history and died of respiratory failure of unknown cause, suggesting a possible familial neuromuscular/metabolic disease background.

The attached phase 1 images show muscle pathology and related electron microscopy images, and the phase 1 text explicitly states that muscle biopsy showed RRF/ragged-blue fibers and abnormal mitochondria, supporting hereditary myopathy or mitochondrial-related myopathy.
opposing_evidence: In the first stage, the female patient herself did not report definite extremity weakness, muscle atrophy, extraocular muscle involvement, or localizing neurologic signs.
In the first stage, no direct evidence was provided for this female patient's pulmonary function, maximal inspiratory pressure/respiratory muscle function, etc.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary arterial hypertension with right heart dysfunction
supporting_evidence: In the first-stage text, the admission diagnosis was "pulmonary hypertension of undetermined etiology, type II respiratory failure"

Physical examination showed moderate cyanosis of the lips while on oxygen, full jugular venous distention when supine, P2>A2, and hepatomegaly, all supporting pulmonary hypertension with right heart involvement
Chest radiograph suggested "cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension"

Echocardiography showed right atrial and right ventricular enlargement, dilation of the main pulmonary artery and right pulmonary artery, mild tricuspid and pulmonic regurgitation, pulmonary artery pressure of 66 mmHg, and moderate to severe pulmonary hypertension.
opposing_evidence: The first-stage information suggests the presence of pulmonary hypertension, but its etiology is unclear; based on the currently available data alone, it is not possible to distinguish primary, heart disease-related, lung disease-related, or hypoventilation-related causes.
There was no edema in either lower extremity at that time, suggesting that the signs of right heart failure were not at their most severe stage.

differential_diagnoses.name: Congenital heart disease-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension/right heart failure (e.g., atrial septal defect, etc.)
supporting_evidence: The first-stage text clearly documented that the patient had previously been diagnosed with "congenital heart disease" in the Department of Cardiology and subsequently in the Department of Respiratory Medicine.

Long-term exertional dyspnea, inability to tolerate ordinary activity, and a history of recurrent hospitalization are consistent with the clinical manifestations of pulmonary arterial hypertension occurring after progression of some congenital shunt heart diseases.

Both the physical examination and ancillary tests showed evidence of increased right heart load and pulmonary hypertension: P2 > A2, right atrial and right ventricular enlargement, and pulmonary artery widening
opposing_evidence: In the first-stage echocardiography, only right atrial and right ventricular enlargement and pulmonary hypertension were noted; specific structural abnormalities such as atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, and patent ductus arteriosus were not clearly reported.
Physical examination did not describe a typical murmur of congenital heart disease

differential_diagnoses.name: chronic cor pulmonale/chronic hypoxic pulmonary hypertension
supporting_evidence: Chest X-ray directly indicates "cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension"
The patient has long-term chest tightness, dyspnea, and cyanosis, with severe hypoxemia and hypercapnia, which may cause or worsen pulmonary vasoconstriction and increased right heart workload.
Physical examination showed jugular venous distention, accentuated P2, hepatomegaly, and bilateral enlargement of the cardiac borders, consistent with decompensated cor pulmonale.
opposing_evidence: In the first stage, no history of chronic cough, sputum production, long-term smoking, definite COPD, or diffuse parenchymal lung disease was provided.
On examination of both lungs, only a few moist rales were present, without typical signs of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary embolism-related right heart strain
supporting_evidence: In the first stage, there was definite pulmonary hypertension, right atrial and right ventricular enlargement, hypoxemia, and dyspnea.

Symptoms are recurrent and prolonged; the etiology of pulmonary hypertension remains to be determined in the first stage, and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension should be included in the differential diagnosis.
opposing_evidence: In the first stage, no risk factors supporting venous thromboembolism were provided, such as lower extremity deep venous thrombosis, sudden chest pain, hemoptysis, prolonged bed rest, or a history of surgery.

The disease course has gradually progressed since 2003, which is more consistent with a chronic process; meanwhile, severe hypercapnia is also atypical and does not support pulmonary embolism alone as the primary cause.

stage2_input.text: New test results after admission: elevated creatine kinase; no significant abnormalities in liver and renal function, electrolytes, myocardial injury markers, complete blood count, coagulation function, thyroid function, hemorheology, routine stool and urine tests, ANCA, ANAS, or anticardiolipin antibody panel. Echocardiography: left ventricular wall thickening, pulmonary artery pressure 45 mmHg (mildly elevated). Ambulatory EEG: normal. Electromyography of all four extremities: normal. Abdominal ultrasound and brain MRI showed no significant abnormalities. ECG was normal. Respiratory function-related tests: both hypoxic ventilatory drive and hypercapnic ventilatory drive of the respiratory center were below the laboratory normal values. Laryngoscopy: deviated nasal septum, pharyngitis. (Day +6543) Daytime blood gas: PH 7.37↓, PO2 57 mmHg ↓, PCO2 47 mmHg↑, SO2 88↓, BE 1.25, CHO3- 27.2↑, LAC 5.91 mmol/L↑. (Day +6547) Pulmonary function report (upright): normal ventilatory function, normal diffusing capacity. Pulmonary function report (supine): mild restrictive ventilatory dysfunction. PSG monitoring: PSG findings consistent with moderate obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome. Predominantly obstructive hypopnea, AHI 23.8 events/h. Lowest oxygen saturation 59%. Blood gas after completion of monitoring: PH 7.34↓, PO2 49 mmHg ↓, PCO2 57 mmHg↑, SO2 83↓, LAC 1.821↑. Manual pressure titration: EEG approximately normal. Titration pressure BIPAP S/T (E: 6, I: 14) cmH20, T 12 breaths/min.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Full-length mitochondrial genome testing: a pathogenic variant that can explain the patient's phenotype was detected.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient and her family have a complete clinical constellation highly suggestive of mitochondrial disease: the female proband developed chest tightness, dyspnea, edema, severe type II respiratory failure, and pulmonary hypertension at age 46, with a history of extremely severe hypercapnia (PCO2 up to 120 mmHg) and elevated lactate; her younger brother has long-standing exercise intolerance, limb weakness, sleep-related hypoventilation/obstructive sleep apnea, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, metabolic cardiomyopathy, and hearing loss, with a prior history of ptosis and facial palsy-like cranial nerve involvement; another older sister also had a similar medical history and died of respiratory failure, suggesting a maternal inheritance tendency and familial aggregation. Previous examinations have already provided important supportive clues, including repeatedly elevated lactate, muscle biopsy showing RRF/ragged blue fibers, and abnormal mitochondria on electron microscopy, indicating that mitochondrial encephalomyopathy is already highly suspected; however, this evidence still mainly remains at the phenotypic and pathologic levels, and molecular genetic evidence is still needed to establish a definitive diagnosis. Full-length mitochondrial genome testing was ordered, with the core purpose of addressing the following clinical questions: first, to identify a pathogenic mtDNA variant that can explain the current multisystem phenotype, thereby establishing the diagnosis of mitochondrial disease, especially within the MELAS spectrum, at the genetic level; second, to distinguish differential diagnoses such as isolated sleep apnea, idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension, primary cardiomyopathy, or other neuromuscular diseases, because the respiratory failure, myocardial involvement, hearing loss, and neuromuscular manifestations in this case require a unified etiologic explanation; third, to provide a basis for subsequent treatment and management, because once a pathogenic variant is identified, it can support mitochondrial disease-related interventions, long-term noninvasive ventilation, and multisystem follow-up, and guide genetic counseling for the family and screening of relatives. Because this case already has pathologic and metabolic evidence but involves multiple systems including the respiratory, cardiac, neurologic, and auditory systems, genetic confirmation is decisive for the final diagnosis, risk assessment, and selection of treatment strategies.

Sleep-related alveolar hypoventilation disorder 4. Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome 5. Metabolic cardiomyopathy 6. Pulmonary arterial hypertension 7. Reflux esophagitis 8. Hyperuricemia 9. Decreased hearing in the left ear 10. Pulmonary opacity
diagnostic_basis: Muscle biopsy: RRF fibers + abnormal mitochondria

Ancillary examinations and laboratory tests: PSG monitoring: PSG findings of moderate obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome. Echocardiography: left ventricular wall thickening, pulmonary artery pressure 45 mmHg (mildly elevated).

treatment_plan: Regular nocturnal use of BiPAP (EPAP 5 cmH2O, IPAP 13 cmH2O, T 12 breaths/min + oxygen 2 L/min
Long-term use of coenzyme Q10 and L-arginine
treatment_response: Follow-up visit on Day +6593: while awake and not receiving oxygen, oxygen saturation could reach 93%.
Reduced sleep efficiency, absence of deep sleep, absence of REM sleep.
PSG findings consistent with mild obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome, AHI 7 events/hour, predominantly hypopnea.
Average oxygen saturation during sleep was 83%, and the lowest oxygen saturation was 66%.
During pressure titration, the patient had repeated ineffective triggering caused by respiratory muscle weakness.
Final titration pressure: BiPAP ST (E: 4, I: 11) cmH2O.
